# Form

The anatomy layer above Field. Field solves one labelled control; Form owns everything around them: the form element and its rhythm, the chapters of a long form, the fieldset, and the bar that closes it.

```tsx
<Form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
  <FormSection>
    <FormSectionHeader>
      <FormSectionTitle>Contact</FormSectionTitle>
      <FormSectionDescription>Where we send the receipt.</FormSectionDescription>
    </FormSectionHeader>

    <FieldRow>
      <Field required>
        <FieldLabel>First name</FieldLabel>
        <InputRoot><InputField placeholder="Ada" /></InputRoot>
      </Field>
      <Field required>
        <FieldLabel>Last name</FieldLabel>
        <InputRoot><InputField placeholder="Lovelace" /></InputRoot>
      </Field>
    </FieldRow>

    <Field required>
      <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
      <InputRoot><InputField type="email" placeholder="ada@example.com" /></InputRoot>
      <FieldHint>We'll only use it for this order.</FieldHint>
    </Field>
  </FormSection>

  <FormSection>
    <FormSectionTitle>Delivery</FormSectionTitle>

    <FieldGroup>
      <FieldGroupLabel>Delivery speed</FieldGroupLabel>
      <RadioGroup defaultValue="standard">
        <RadioCard value="standard">
          <RadioCardTitle>Standard</RadioCardTitle>
          <RadioCardDescription>Free, 4 to 6 business days</RadioCardDescription>
        </RadioCard>
        <RadioCard value="express">
          <RadioCardTitle>Express</RadioCardTitle>
          <RadioCardDescription>$12.00, 1 to 2 business days</RadioCardDescription>
        </RadioCard>
      </RadioGroup>
    </FieldGroup>
  </FormSection>

  <FormActions bordered>
    <Button type="button" variant="ghost">Cancel</Button>
    <Button type="submit">Place order</Button>
  </FormActions>
</Form>
```

## Installation

```bash
# One-time setup (tokens + lib helpers)
npx koalaui-cli init

# Add this component (its dependencies come along)
npx koalaui-cli add form
```

Manual: run `npm install radix-ui tailwind-variants tailwind-merge`, then copy the source into `components/ui/form/` and adjust the import paths to your project. Components pull `cn` from `lib/utils`, the `tv` wrapper from `lib/tv`, and (for multi-part components) `createContext` from `lib/create-context`.

## Anatomy

Every part answers one question: how many controls does this wrap, and what is it to the reader? Get that right and the spacing, the labelling, and the ARIA all follow without a decision.

| Part | Wraps |
| --- | --- |
| `Form` | The <form> element itself. Owns the vertical rhythm and the height of every control inside it. |
| `Field` | One labelled control. Generates the id / htmlFor / aria-describedby wiring and cascades error and disabled state. |
| `FieldGroup` | Several controls answering one question (a radio set, a checkbox cluster). A real fieldset + legend. |
| `FieldRow` | Two or three fields that belong on one line. Stacks to a single column below sm. |
| `FormSection` | A chapter of a long form, with its own title and description. Gets extra air from the chapter before it, and can set the header beside the fields with layout="split". |
| `FormActions` | The bar that closes the form. Aligns the buttons, optionally rules itself off from the fields above. |
| `InputGroup` | Several controls fused into ONE bordered box (a currency prefix, a url + select). Sits inside a Field, not beside one. |

The line that trips people up is `Field` versus `FieldGroup`. A single “I agree to the terms” checkbox is one control, so it is a `Field`. Three checkboxes picking email preferences answer one question, so they are a `FieldGroup`. And `InputGroup` is not a layout part at all: it fuses several controls into one bordered box, so it lives *inside* a Field where a single control would otherwise go.

## Usage

`Form` renders a plain `form` element, so `action`, `onSubmit`, and server actions all work exactly as they do on the native element. What it adds is the rhythm, so no form in your app has to invent its own gap.

```tsx
import { Form, FormActions } from "@/components/ui/form"
import { Field, FieldLabel } from "@/components/ui/field"

<Form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
  <Field required>
    <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
    <InputRoot><InputField type="email" /></InputRoot>
  </Field>

  <FormActions>
    <Button variant="ghost">Cancel</Button>
    <Button type="submit">Continue</Button>
  </FormActions>
</Form>
```

## Control size

A form field is the thing being filled in, not a control tucked into a toolbar, so a Form sets its controls to `lg` (40px) by default. That is the top of the band the industry settled on: shadcn/ui ships a 36px input, Carbon's large is 48px, and touch guidance puts the comfortable range at 32 to 40px with a 44px hit area. 32px reads cramped for something you type into.

One prop retunes the whole form, fields and buttons together, so they can never mismatch. A control's own `size` still wins where you need one exception.

```tsx
<Form size="sm">…</Form>   {/* 32px */}
<Form size="md">…</Form>   {/* 36px */}
<Form>…</Form>             {/* 40px, the default */}
```

Reach for `sm` when the form is really a dense app surface: a filter bar above a table, a settings row inside a compact shell. Everything else, a signup, a checkout, a contact block, wants the default.

## Rhythm and density

Density and size are two different axes, and keeping them apart is what stops a form from drifting. `size` is how tall the controls are; `density` is how much space sits between them. The gap comes from the same axis that tunes every other gap in Koala: `compact` (the default) is 16px, `comfortable` is 20px.

```tsx
<Form density="compact">…</Form>
<Form density="comfortable">…</Form>
```

## Sections

Once a form is long enough to have chapters, wrap each one in a `FormSection`. Sections keep the field rhythm inside themselves and take extra air from the section before them, so a chapter break reads as a break without you reaching for a margin.

```tsx
<Form>
  <FormSection>
    <FormSectionHeader>
      <FormSectionTitle>Account</FormSectionTitle>
      <FormSectionDescription>How you sign in.</FormSectionDescription>
    </FormSectionHeader>
    <Field>…</Field>
  </FormSection>

  <FormSection>
    <FormSectionHeader>
      <FormSectionTitle>Profile</FormSectionTitle>
      <FormSectionDescription>Shown on your public page.</FormSectionDescription>
    </FormSectionHeader>
    <Field>…</Field>
    <Field>…</Field>
  </FormSection>
</Form>
```

`FormSectionTitle` renders an `h3`. When that is the wrong level for the page outline, pass `asChild` and bring your own heading: `<FormSectionTitle asChild><h2>Shipping</h2></FormSectionTitle>`.

`layout="split"` sets the header *beside* the fields instead of above them: the settings row you know from Stripe, Linear, and Tailwind UI. It stacks back to one column below `md`. Split sections need a `FormSectionBody` around the fields, because in a grid each field would otherwise claim a cell of its own instead of sharing the column.

```tsx
<FormSection layout="split" density="comfortable" className="border-t border-border py-8">
  <FormSectionHeader>
    <FormSectionTitle className="text-base">Profile</FormSectionTitle>
    <FormSectionDescription>This information is shown to your teammates.</FormSectionDescription>
  </FormSectionHeader>
  <FormSectionBody density="comfortable">
    <Field>…</Field>
    <Field>…</Field>
  </FormSectionBody>
</FormSection>
```

A section is also the form body where a `form` element can't go: inside a Dialog the actions belong to `DialogFooter`, so there is nothing to submit. There it stays pure layout, which keeps the fields the same height as the dialog's own buttons. Pass `size` on the section if you want the taller form controls anyway, or to give one chapter a different height from the rest.

## Field groups

When several controls answer one question, a label has nothing to point at: there is no single control to name. `FieldGroup` is a real `fieldset` and `FieldGroupLabel` a real `legend`, which is the one construct that names a set of controls with no ARIA at all. The hint below works the same as in a Field, and describes the whole group.

```tsx
<FieldGroup>
  <FieldGroupLabel required>Email preferences</FieldGroupLabel>
  <div className="flex flex-col gap-2.5">
    <label className="flex items-center gap-2.5 text-sm">
      <Checkbox defaultChecked />
      Product updates
    </label>
    <label className="flex items-center gap-2.5 text-sm">
      <Checkbox />
      Weekly digest
    </label>
  </div>
  <FieldHint>Pick at least one. You can change this any time.</FieldHint>
</FieldGroup>
```

`hasError` turns the hint into an error message, exactly as on a Field. `disabled` is the native fieldset attribute, so it disables every control nested inside without a single prop being passed down.

```tsx
<FieldGroup hasError>
  <FieldGroupLabel required>Delivery speed</FieldGroupLabel>
  <RadioGroup>…</RadioGroup>
  <FieldHint>Choose a delivery speed to continue.</FieldHint>
</FieldGroup>

<FieldGroup disabled>
  <FieldGroupLabel>Delivery speed</FieldGroupLabel>
  <RadioGroup defaultValue="standard">…</RadioGroup>
  <FieldHint>Delivery is set by your plan.</FieldHint>
</FieldGroup>
```

Do not add an `aria-label` to the control inside a group. The legend already names the set, and a second name only makes a screen reader say it twice.

## Rows

`FieldRow` puts fields that belong together on one line, and stacks them to a single column below `sm` so nothing gets cramped. It takes `columns` of 2 (the default) or 3.

```tsx
<FieldRow>
  <Field>…</Field>
  <Field>…</Field>
</FieldRow>

<FieldRow columns={3}>
  <Field>…</Field>
  <Field>…</Field>
  <Field>…</Field>
</FieldRow>
```

## Actions

`FormActions` closes the form. `end` (the default) is the ghost + primary pairing; `between` pushes a destructive action away from the primary one; `stack` is the full-width submit a signup or checkout wants. Add `bordered` when the form is long enough that the bar needs a seam, and put a status message in as a first child with `mr-auto`.

```tsx
<FormActions>
  <Button variant="ghost">Cancel</Button>
  <Button>Save changes</Button>
</FormActions>

<FormActions align="between">
  <Button variant="destructiveGhost">Delete</Button>
  <Button>Save changes</Button>
</FormActions>

<FormActions align="stack">
  <Button>Create account</Button>
</FormActions>

<FormActions bordered>
  <span className="mr-auto text-sm font-medium text-success">All changes saved</span>
  <Button variant="ghost">Cancel</Button>
  <Button>Save changes</Button>
</FormActions>
```

## One-line capture

A newsletter or waitlist form is one field and one button, not a column. `layout="row"` is that shape: the field grows, the button hugs, and the pair stacks below `sm`. It is the same layout `NewsletterForm` and `WaitlistForm` use, so the three can never drift apart.

```tsx
<Form layout="row" onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
  {/* w-full, not flex-1: flex-1 collapses the field's height when the row stacks. */}
  <InputRoot className="w-full">
    <InputPrefix><EnvelopeSimple weight="bold" /></InputPrefix>
    <InputField type="email" placeholder="you@company.com" aria-label="Work email" />
  </InputRoot>
  <Button type="submit" className="shrink-0 max-sm:w-full">Subscribe</Button>
</Form>
```

There is a third layout, `plain`, for when the form element *is* a card whose header, body, and footer sit flush against its borders. It contributes no rhythm at all, leaving a `FormSection` inside to own the field spacing. `SettingsForm` is built that way.

## Validation: bring your own

Form ships no validation, no schema prop, and no state. That is deliberate: most teams have already picked a form library or are using server actions, and a design system that insists on its own choice is one you have to fight. Field already exposes the surface validation needs, `hasError` and a `FieldHint` that doubles as the error message, so wiring any resolver is a few lines.

```tsx
// react-hook-form
const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm()

<Form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onValid)}>
  <Field required hasError={!!errors.email}>
    <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
    <InputRoot><InputField {...register("email", { required: true })} /></InputRoot>
    <FieldHint>{errors.email ? "Enter a valid email." : "We'll send a receipt here."}</FieldHint>
  </Field>
  <FormActions><Button type="submit">Continue</Button></FormActions>
</Form>
```

```tsx
// Server action, no client library at all
const [state, action] = useActionState(subscribe, {})

<Form action={action}>
  <Field required hasError={!!state.errors?.email}>
    <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
    <InputRoot><InputField name="email" type="email" /></InputRoot>
    <FieldHint>{state.errors?.email ?? "We'll send a receipt here."}</FieldHint>
  </Field>
  <FormActions><Button type="submit">Continue</Button></FormActions>
</Form>
```

## FAQ

### When do I use Field and when do I use FieldGroup?

Count the controls that answer the question. One control is a Field, so a single 'I agree to the terms' checkbox is a Field. Several controls answering one question is a FieldGroup, so a radio set or a cluster of preference checkboxes is a FieldGroup. The difference matters for more than spacing: a group has no single control for a label to point at, which is why FieldGroup renders a real fieldset and legend.

### Why does FieldGroup use fieldset and legend instead of ARIA?

A fieldset with a legend is the one construct in HTML that names a set of controls with no ARIA at all, and its disabled attribute natively disables everything nested inside it, so FieldGroup disabled needs to pass nothing down to the controls. Reaching for role='group' plus aria-labelledby would reimplement, badly, what the browser already does.

### Does Form handle validation?

No, and that is deliberate. Form renders a plain form element and owns layout and semantics only, so react-hook-form, Formik, server actions, or nothing at all all work unchanged. Field already gives validation everything it needs: set hasError on the Field and put the message in the FieldHint.

### What gap should I use between fields?

None of your own: Form owns it. The gap comes from density, compact at 16px (the default) and comfortable at 20px, which is the same axis that tunes every other gap in Koala. If you find yourself adding a margin between fields, you probably want a FormSection instead.

### Why are form controls taller than the same control elsewhere?

Because a Form sets its controls to lg (40px) by default, while a bare control follows density and lands at 32px in a compact shell. A field you type into is not the same as a control tucked into a toolbar, and 40px is the top of the band the industry uses: shadcn/ui ships 36px, Carbon's medium is 40px, and touch guidance wants 40px or a 44px hit area. Pass size on the Form to change it for the whole form at once.

### How do I make one control a different size from the rest of the form?

Put size on that control. The precedence runs most-local-first: the control's own size beats an explicit density on the control, which beats the size the Form imposes, which beats the ambient density. So the Form's size is a default, never an override, and a single field can opt out without you rewriting the form.

### Does density still affect control heights?

Only outside a Form. Density picks the default size for a bare control (compact picks sm, comfortable picks md), but inside a Form the Form's size wins, so the two axes stop fighting: size is how tall the controls are, density is how much space sits between them.

### Can I put a Form inside a Dialog?

Yes, and context follows the component tree rather than the DOM, so all the Field wiring keeps working through Radix's Portal. Use DialogFooter rather than FormActions for the dialog's buttons: an overlay's actions reverse to a stacked column on mobile so the primary action sits under the thumb, which is a different rule from a form in the page flow.

### How is InputGroup different from FieldRow?

FieldRow is layout: separate fields, each with its own label and border, laid side by side. InputGroup is a single control surface: several controls fused into ONE bordered box with hairline seams between them, like a currency prefix beside an amount. An InputGroup goes inside a Field, where one control would otherwise sit.

### Do I still need aria-label on a RadioGroup inside a FieldGroup?

No. The legend names the set, and adding an aria-label on the control gives it a second name that a screen reader will read out twice. A RadioGroup dropped into a plain Field is the case that does need the wiring, and it gets it automatically: because a RadioGroup renders a div that htmlFor cannot name, it picks up aria-labelledby from the Field's label instead.

## Exports and dependencies

`npx koalaui-cli add form` writes `components/ui/form/`. Import from `@/components/ui/form`:

- Components and helpers: `Form`, `FormSection`, `FormSectionHeader`, `FormSectionBody`, `FormSectionTitle`, `FormSectionDescription`, `FormActions`, `formVariants`
- Types: `FormProps`, `FormSectionProps`, `FormSectionBodyProps`, `FormSectionTitleProps`, `FormActionsProps`
- Koala components it installs with it: `field`
- Koala lib helpers it uses: `density`, `tv`
- npm packages: `radix-ui`
